[Aristotle](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fm%2F0gz_&q=Aristotle) wrote this famous reflection at the very end of his work Sophistical Refutations (Sophistici Elenchi), concluding his collection of logical treatises known as the Organon. [1]
In this closing passage, he proudly points out that while other subjects (like rhetoric) had a long history of foundational work he could build upon, he had to invent the study of formal deduction (the syllogism) entirely from scratch. [1]
The exact quote, in a common English translation, reads:
"Of the present inquiry, on the other hand, it was not the case that part of the work had been thoroughly done before, while part had not. Nothing existed at all… On the subject of deduction [syllogizing] we had absolutely nothing else of an earlier date to mention, but were kept at work for a long time in experimental researches." [1]
Why Aristotle Made This Claim

* The Invention of Formal Logic: Before Aristotle, philosophers like Plato and the Sophists argued using logic implicitly, but no one had analyzed the structure of arguments. Aristotle isolated the mechanics of reasoning into what we now call syllogistic logic—the process of deriving a necessary conclusion from two premises (e.g., All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; therefore, Socrates is mortal).
* Contrasting Rhetoric: In the same passage, Aristotle notes that teachers of rhetoric (like Gorgias) simply gave their students ready-made speeches to memorize. Aristotle wanted to give his students the actual system or tool (Organon) to evaluate any argument's validity on their own. [[1], [2], [3], [4]]

Would you like to explore how Aristotle defined the rules of the syllogism in his Prior Analytics, or are you interested in how his logical works were grouped together by later scholars? [[1], [2]]

The archive's account of the claim is concentrated in two defining papers, #1574 and #1603, with #1576 and #1575 naming it as the originality claim at the close of the Topics–SE inquiry and stating the received reading at full strength. Everything else admitted restates, indexes or audits those (the First Draft notebook, #1611, #1684, #1579) or ties the maker-count hypothesis to the claim (#1569, #1571, #1576 §9.4).

The archive is not uniform on practice and art: #1570 §0A.2 holds that '"Practice versus art" is not a modern rescue. It is Aristotle's own frame, in this passage', and #1575 §I ¶3 states the conventional reading as 'about a systematic art'; #1603 §4 answers that the shoemaker 'does not oppose the organized to the raw; it opposes the art to its products'. Carried as its own lineage, marked contested within the pool.
